Why different water purifiers are used

Household water-treatment devices use different methods to reduce different kinds of impurities. Some mainly remove suspended particles, some reduce microorganisms, and others can remove certain dissolved substances.

No single household purifier should be assumed to remove every possible contaminant. The most suitable system depends on the quality of the incoming water and the specific impurities that need to be controlled.

Common types of household treatment

Sediment filters and ceramic filters

A sediment filter removes particles such as sand, rust flakes and silt. Ceramic filters also work by retaining particles in their pores.

The ability of a ceramic filter to remove microorganisms depends on its pore size and design. Basic sediment filters do not reliably remove dissolved salts or all disease-causing microorganisms.

Activated carbon filters

Activated carbon has a large internal surface to which certain substances can attach. This process is called adsorption.

Activated carbon is commonly used to improve the taste and smell of drinking water and to reduce chlorine and some organic substances.

Its main purpose should not be confused with complete disinfection. An ordinary activated-carbon filter is not a reliable standalone method for removing all pathogens or dissolved mineral salts.

Ultrafiltration

Ultrafiltration, abbreviated as UF, passes water through a membrane with very small pores.

Suitable UF membranes can remove bacteria and protozoan parasites. Their effectiveness against viruses is more variable because viruses are smaller than most bacteria and parasites.

UF does not ordinarily remove dissolved salts and many dissolved chemicals. It therefore cannot be assumed to correct excessive salinity or harmful concentrations of dissolved ions.

Ultraviolet purification

Ultraviolet purification, abbreviated as UV, uses UV light to inactivate microorganisms by damaging their ability to reproduce or cause infection.

UV is a disinfection method, not a method for physically filtering out dissolved substances. Effective UV treatment requires suitable equipment and water clear enough for the light to reach the microorganisms.

Therefore, UV purification does not reduce dissolved salts or total dissolved solids merely by exposing water to light.

Reverse osmosis

Reverse osmosis, abbreviated as RO, uses a membrane that allows water to pass while rejecting a substantial proportion of dissolved salts and certain other contaminants.

Suitable RO systems can reduce dissolved salts and several chemical contaminants. Properly functioning RO membranes also provide an effective barrier to many microorganisms. However, the exact performance depends on the system, membrane condition, installation and maintenance.

RO is particularly relevant when the water contains excessive dissolved salts or specific chemical contaminants that the selected system is designed to reduce.

Not every household needs RO treatment. If water is already safe and meets applicable quality requirements, RO may provide little additional benefit for the particular water source.

Comparison of household purification methods

MethodMain useImportant limitation
Sediment or basic ceramic filterReduces suspended particlesDoes not remove dissolved salts; microbial removal depends on design
Activated carbonImproves taste and odour; reduces chlorine and some organic substancesNot reliable as the sole disinfection method
UFRemoves bacteria and protozoan parasites with suitable membranesDoes not remove dissolved salts; virus reduction varies
UVInactivates microorganismsDoes not remove dissolved salts or other chemicals
ROReduces dissolved salts and selected contaminantsRemoval performance depends on the particular system
Water softenerReduces hardness caused mainly by calcium and magnesiumDoes not reliably remove disease-causing microorganisms

Hardness, salinity and contamination are different problems

Hard water contains appreciable quantities of dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. These can cause scale deposits and reduce the effectiveness of soap.

Saline water contains dissolved salts that may make the water taste salty. The dissolved substances responsible for hardness and those responsible for salinity need not be identical.

Microbial contamination refers to the presence of potentially harmful microorganisms. It can occur even when the water is neither hard nor noticeably salty.

The concentration of total dissolved solids, or TDS, indicates the amount of dissolved material in water. It does not directly establish whether harmful bacteria or viruses are present.

UV addresses microorganisms; UF separates suitable microorganisms by membrane filtration; RO reduces dissolved salts. The methods are not interchangeable simply because all are used in household water purifiers.

How the water problem determines the treatment

If water contains visible suspended particles, appropriate settling or filtration may be necessary. If harmful microorganisms are the concern, a suitable disinfection or validated pathogen-removal method is needed. If testing identifies excessive dissolved salts or a particular chemical contaminant, the selected treatment must be capable of reducing that substance.

Some household systems combine sediment filtration, activated carbon, UF, UV or RO because the incoming water may have more than 1 type of problem.

Maintenance is part of water safety

Filters and membranes can become clogged, damaged or ineffective. Activated-carbon media can lose their capacity to reduce particular substances. UV lamps and other components also require appropriate maintenance.

Regular cleaning, timely replacement of consumable parts and hygienic storage are therefore important. The performance claims of a purifier should be checked against the contaminants actually present in the water.

Public drinking-water programmes in India and Gujarat

Household purification is only 1 part of drinking-water safety. Public water-supply systems also need reliable sources, appropriate treatment, distribution and quality monitoring.

The Government of India's Jal Jeevan Mission is directed toward providing rural households with functional tap connections supplying water meeting the Bureau of Indian Standards drinking-water standard IS 10500, at a minimum of 55 litres per person per day and on a regular basis. It is a public drinking-water service initiative, not a particular RO or UV technology.

In Gujarat, the Water and Sanitation Management Organisation, known as WASMO, has promoted community participation in rural drinking-water service delivery and management.

These initiatives illustrate the importance of safe water supply at the community level. Their names should not be confused with the names of individual household purification methods.

The programme descriptions above are based on the respective official institutional information consulted on 3 November 2026. No current household-coverage percentage or completion claim is made here.

Prelims focus

  • UV treatment inactivates microorganisms but does not remove dissolved salts.
  • UF membranes can remove bacteria and protozoan parasites; virus removal varies.
  • RO reduces dissolved salts and certain chemical contaminants.
  • Activated carbon is commonly used to improve taste and odour.
  • Water hardness is associated mainly with calcium and magnesium.
  • Trap: A TDS reading alone cannot establish whether water is free from harmful microorganisms.

[Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, About Home Water Treatment Systems, 10 April 2024, sections on ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis, ultraviolet treatment and water softeners, consulted 3 November 2026; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, About Choosing Home Water Filters, sections on taste, germs and chemicals, consulted 3 November 2026; Ministry of Jal Shakti, Jal Jeevan Mission, About JJM, official website, consulted 3 November 2026; Water and Sanitation Management Organisation, Gujarat, About Us, official website, consulted 3 November 2026.]
